title: Photoelectrical readout and Ramsey interferometry of single shallowly implanted NV centers in diamond
authors: Ilia Chuprina, Christoph Findler, Johannes Lang, Petr Siyushev, Fedor Jelezko
abstract: Photoelectrical readout of the electronic spin state of the nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond is attracting significant interest due to the numerous advantages it possesses compared with conventional fluorescence readout. The higher charge carrier rate compared to the photon rate and the integration of the detection scheme on a chip can significantly advance quantum sensing and computing with color centers in diamond. Until now, photoelectric readout has been performed on ensembles of NV centers or single NV centers deep in ultrapure diamond substrates. However, many applications require the artificial creation and precise placement of shallow NV centers, and photoelectric detection of such centers has been challenging. Here we demonstrate photoelectrical readout and coherent control of the electronic spin of implanted shallow ($\sim$10 nm) NV centers buried by diamond overgrowth. The photoelectrically measured Ramsey $T_2^*$ agrees with conventional fluorescence readout and shows no measurable dependence on the readout photocurrent, for both shallow implanted and deep ingrown NV centers. We further find that overgrowth improves photoelectric readout by suppressing the background photocurrent. These results establish photoelectric readout as a viable route to chip-integrated, electrically detected nanoscale sensing and to spin registers based on engineered shallow NV centers.
summary: The researchers successfully demonstrated photoelectrical readout and coherent control of single NV centers implanted near the surface of diamond. By using photocurrent measurements instead of fluorescence, they proved that these engineered shallow qubits can be read out electrically with coherence times matching deep centers. This breakthrough paves the way for integrating quantum sensing and computing components onto semiconductor chips.
main_problem: The primary challenge is demonstrating reliable photoelectrical readout and coherent control of single, shallowly implanted Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond.
main_result: Photoelectric readout was successfully demonstrated for shallow NV centers, showing that the measured Ramsey coherence time agrees with conventional fluorescence measurements. This establishes PE readout as a viable route for chip-integrated quantum sensing.
method: The study uses photoelectrical detection (measuring photocurrent) to read out spin states and measure dephasing times ($T_2^*$) via pulsed microwave sequences like Ramsey interferometry.
model_or_system: The system is single NV centers in diamond, specifically focusing on those that have been artificially implanted at shallow depths ($\sim 10$ nm) and subsequently covered by overgrowth. Measurements compare these to naturally occurring (ingrown) deep centers.
key_observables: Ramsey dephasing time ($T_2^*$), spin contrast (photocurrent vs. fluorescence), Rabi oscillation visibility, and background photocurrent levels.
important_parameters: Shallow implantation depth ($\sim 10$ nm), overgrowth thickness, applied bias voltage ($\pm 3 	ext{ V}$), and laser power/duration optimization.
main_assumptions: The PE readout assumes that the spin-dependent charge conversion mechanism is robust against background photocurrents from defects, which are mitigated by diamond overgrowth.
figures_summary: Figures show optical/photoelectrical confocal imaging, pulsed ODMR and Rabi measurements comparing implanted vs. ingrown centers, and Ramsey $T_2^*$ decay curves demonstrating agreement between PE and PL readouts.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the feasibility of PE readout for shallow NVs, confirming coherence times match optical methods, then detailing the measurement techniques (Rabi/Ramsey), and finally discussing how overgrowth improves signal quality while noting power-dependent decoherence effects.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses hardware implementation challenges in solid-state quantum memories. The ability to use electrical detection for spin readout is crucial for scalable, chip-based quantum devices, providing a pathway beyond purely optical methods.

NV sensing of materials.note: This paper directly uses NV centers in diamond to measure coherence times ($T_2^*$) via pulsed microwave sequences, which is a core technique for quantum relaxometry and probing local spin environments in condensed matter.
